account: Copenhagen Emergency Medical Services used a machine-learning framework to listen to calls to the 112 emergency number and flag suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest for dispatchers. In a retrospective study of 108,607 calls from 2014, the authors found that the model recognized cardiac arrest with higher sensitivity than dispatchers (84.1% versus 72.5%). Its specificity was lower (97.3% versus 98.8%). It was also faster (median 44 versus 54 seconds). A double-masked randomized trial of 169,049 calls ran from 1 September 2018 to 31 December 2019. The trial authors found that dispatchers recognized 93.1% of confirmed arrests with alerts and 90.5% without, a difference that was not significant (P = .15). Alerts alone were more sensitive than dispatchers (85.0% versus 77.5%). The alerts had lower specificity (97.4% versus 99.6%) and a lower positive predictive value (17.8% versus 55.8%). In a project report published on 13 January 2020, staff of the European Emergency Number Association and Corti name the framework as Corti's. In a 2023 paper, authors from Copenhagen Emergency Medical Services report that the model processed 169,236 calls during the trial period with 84.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity. They report that many of its misses involved reports of normal breathing or language barriers. The ethicist Elisabeth Hildt argued in 2025 that the dispatchers tended to ignore the alerts. In a scoping review of 24 September 2026, Yonsei University researchers rated the trial as having some concerns for risk of bias. No source documents an outcome for an individual patient that is attributable to an alert.

ai_role.statement: The AI listened to live calls and alerted dispatchers. In the randomized trial its alerts were more sensitive than dispatchers alone (85.0% vs 77.5%). They did not significantly change dispatcher recognition (93.1% vs 90.5%, P = .15). The benefit is thus a demonstrated detection capability, not a verified change in any patient's course.

fields.account: Copenhagen Emergency Medical Services used a machine-learning framework to listen to calls to the 112 emergency number and flag suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest for dispatchers. In a retrospective study of 108,607 calls from 2014, the authors found that the model recognized cardiac arrest with higher sensitivity than dispatchers (84.1% versus 72.5%). Its specificity was lower (97.3% versus 98.8%). It was also faster (median 44 versus 54 seconds). A double-masked randomized trial of 169,049 calls ran from 1 September 2018 to 31 December 2019. The trial authors found that dispatchers recognized 93.1% of confirmed arrests with alerts and 90.5% without, a difference that was not significant (P = .15). Alerts alone were more sensitive than dispatchers (85.0% versus 77.5%). The alerts had lower specificity (97.4% versus 99.6%) and a lower positive predictive value (17.8% versus 55.8%). In a project report published on 13 January 2020, staff of the European Emergency Number Association and Corti name the framework as Corti's. In a 2023 paper, authors from Copenhagen Emergency Medical Services report that the model processed 169,236 calls during the trial period with 84.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity. They report that many of its misses involved reports of normal breathing or language barriers. The ethicist Elisabeth Hildt argued in 2025 that the dispatchers tended to ignore the alerts. In a scoping review of 24 September 2026, Yonsei University researchers rated the trial as having some concerns for risk of bias. No source documents an outcome for an individual patient that is attributable to an alert.
